source_title: Great Living Chola Temples
text: The Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur, also known as the Big Temple or Brihadeeswarar Temple, is a Hindu temple dedicated to Shiva. It was built by the Chola emperor Rajaraja I in the early 11th century CE, with inscriptions marking its completion around 1010 CE. The temple is part of the UNESCO World Heritage property 'Great Living Chola Temples'. Its vimana, the tower above the sanctum, rises to about 66 metres and is among the tallest temple towers of its period, built from interlocking granite blocks without mortar. The temple complex also houses a massive Nandi statue and preserves Chola-era inscriptions and paintings.

source_title: Great Living Chola Temples
text: Granite for the Brihadisvara Temple was not available locally and had to be transported from quarries roughly 50 kilometres away. The temple's inscriptions record details of its endowments, administration, and the artisans involved in its construction. The temple remains in active worship today, which is reflected in its inclusion among the 'Great Living Chola Temples'.

source_title: Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram
text: The Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram (Mamallapuram) on the Coromandel Coast of Tamil Nadu is part of the UNESCO World Heritage property 'Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram'. It was built in the 8th century CE during the reign of the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II, also known as Rajasimha. It is one of the earliest structural stone temples in South India, meaning it was built from assembled stone blocks rather than being carved out of living rock. The temple complex faces the Bay of Bengal and includes shrines dedicated to Shiva.

source_title: Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram
text: Located directly on the seashore, the Shore Temple has endured centuries of exposure to wind and salt spray from the Bay of Bengal. Mahabalipuram was a major port city of the Pallava dynasty, and its monuments include chariot-shaped rathas, cave sanctuaries, and giant open-air reliefs such as the Descent of the Ganges, reflecting Pallava art and religion.

source_title: Sun Temple, Konârak
text: The Sun Temple at Konark, Odisha, is a UNESCO World Heritage property inscribed as 'Sun Temple, Konârak'. It was built in the 13th century CE, around 1250, during the reign of King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty. Dedicated to Surya, the Hindu Sun god, the temple was conceived as a colossal stone chariot with 24 intricately carved wheels and seven horses, symbolizing the Sun's journey across the sky. It is a masterpiece of Kalinga architecture.

source_title: Sun Temple, Konârak
text: The Konark temple is renowned for its elaborate stone sculpture, including figures and decorative motifs covering its walls. Much of the main temple structure has fallen into ruin over the centuries, while the audience hall, known as the jagamohana, remains standing. The site continues to be associated with the worship of Surya and with the cultural heritage of Odisha.

source_title: Historic City of Madurai
text: The Meenakshi Amman Temple in Madurai, Tamil Nadu, is a historic Hindu temple dedicated to the goddess Meenakshi (a form of Parvati) and her consort Sundareswarar (a form of Shiva). The temple complex is one of the most important pilgrimage sites in South India and is renowned for its towering gopurams (gateway towers) covered in thousands of colourful sculpted figures. The present structure largely dates to the 16th–17th century CE under the Nayaka dynasty, though the temple's origins are older. It is a major example of Dravidian architecture.

source_title: Historic City of Madurai
text: The Meenakshi Temple's thousand-pillared hall and its massive gopurams are defining features of Dravidian temple architecture. The annual Meenakshi Thirukalyanam festival celebrates the divine marriage of Meenakshi and Sundareswarar and draws hundreds of thousands of devotees. The temple complex is laid out in concentric square enclosures and sits at the heart of the ancient city of Madurai.

source_title: The Jagannath Temple, Puri
text: The Jagannath Temple in Puri, Odisha, is one of the Char Dham pilgrimage sites sacred to Hindus. Dedicated to Jagannath (a form of Krishna/Vishnu), the temple was rebuilt in the 12th century CE by King Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva of the Eastern Ganga dynasty. The temple is famous for its annual Rath Yatra (chariot festival), during which the deities are placed on enormous wooden chariots and pulled through the streets by devotees.

source_title: The Jagannath Temple, Puri
text: The Jagannath Temple follows Kalinga architectural style, with a tall curvilinear spire (deula) over the sanctum. The temple kitchen is reputed to be among the largest in the world, preparing the Mahaprasad offering cooked in earthen pots over wood fire. The temple remains in active worship and is an important centre of Odia culture and heritage.

source_title: Kashi Vishwanath Temple, Varanasi
text: The Kashi Vishwanath Temple in Varanasi (Kashi), Uttar Pradesh, is one of the most famous Hindu temples dedicated to Shiva. Located on the western bank of the Ganges River, Varanasi is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and is considered a sacred city in Hinduism. The present temple structure was rebuilt in the 18th century CE by Queen Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore, though a temple on this site is much older.

source_title: Kashi Vishwanath Temple, Varanasi
text: The Kashi Vishwanath Temple's spire is gold-plated, and the temple complex includes smaller shrines and the Jnana Vapi (Wisdom Well). Varanasi's ghats along the Ganges and its temples make the city a major pilgrimage centre. The temple is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas, considered especially sacred shrines of Shiva.

source_title: Great Living Chola Temples
text: The Chola dynasty was a Tamil dynasty that ruled parts of southern India from roughly the 9th to the 13th century CE. Under rulers such as Rajaraja I and Rajendra I, the Cholas built monumental temples including the Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur and the Brihadisvara Temple at Gangaikonda Cholapuram. Chola architecture is characterised by massive vimanas, elaborate stone sculpture, and inscriptions that record administration, endowments, and trade.

source_title: Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram
text: The Pallava dynasty ruled parts of southern India from roughly the 6th to the 9th century CE, with its capital at Kanchipuram and an important port at Mahabalipuram. Pallava architecture includes both rock-cut monuments (such as the Pancha Rathas and cave sanctuaries at Mahabalipuram) and early structural stone temples such as the Shore Temple. Pallava art influenced later Dravidian temple architecture and also spread to Southeast Asia.

source_title: Great Living Chola Temples
text: Dravidian architecture is the temple-building tradition of South India, characterised by a pyramidal tower (vimana) over the sanctum, pillared halls (mandapas), an enclosing wall (prakara), and monumental gateway towers (gopurams). Chola temples such as the Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur exemplify mature Dravidian architecture with massive granite vimanas and detailed inscriptions.

source_title: Sun Temple, Konârak
text: Kalinga architecture is the temple-building tradition of Odisha and nearby regions, characterised by a curvilinear tower (deula) over the sanctum, a rectangular assembly hall (jagamohana), and elaborate stone sculpture. The Sun Temple at Konark, conceived as a stone chariot with carved wheels and horses, is a celebrated example of Kalinga architecture.

source_title: World Heritage Centre
text: UNESCO's World Heritage Convention identifies and protects cultural and natural heritage of outstanding universal value to humanity. India has numerous properties inscribed on the World Heritage List, including the Great Living Chola Temples, the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, and the Sun Temple at Konark. The convention encourages conservation, monitoring, and international cooperation to safeguard these sites for future generations.

source_title: The Jagannath Temple, Puri
text: The Rath Yatra or chariot festival at the Jagannath Temple in Puri is one of the largest and oldest Hindu festivals. During the festival, the deities Jagannath, Balabhadra, and Subhadra are taken from the temple in enormous wooden chariots to the Gundicha Temple, about three kilometres away, where they remain for several days before returning. The festival attracts millions of devotees and is a significant expression of Odia religious and cultural heritage.

source_title: Great Living Chola Temples
text: Tamil Nadu, on the southeastern coast of India, is home to thousands of Hindu temples and some of the oldest continuous temple-building traditions in the country. The state's heritage includes the Great Living Chola Temples (Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur, Brihadisvara Temple at Gangaikonda Cholapuram, and Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram), the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, and the Meenakshi Temple in Madurai. Tamil Nadu's temples reflect Chola, Pallava, Pandya, and Nayaka architectural traditions.

source_title: Sun Temple, Konârak
text: Odisha, on the eastern coast of India, is renowned for its Kalinga-style Hindu temples. The state's heritage includes the Sun Temple at Konark, the Jagannath Temple in Puri, and the Lingaraja Temple in Bhubaneswar. These temples are distinguished by their curvilinear spires (deula), assembly halls (jagamohana), and extensive stone carving. Odisha's temples are active centres of worship and important pilgrimage destinations.

source_title: Khajuraho Group of Monuments
text: UNESCO states that Khajuraho's group of temples represents a culmination of northern Indian temple art and architecture associated with the Chandella dynasty, which ruled the region in the 10th and 11th centuries CE. The source describes the group and period; it does not assign an individual construction date to every temple.

source_title: Mahabodhi Temple Complex at Bodh Gaya
text: UNESCO identifies Mahabodhi as one of the four holy sites associated with the Buddha's life, particularly his enlightenment. It describes the present temple as dating to the 5th–6th centuries CE and as one of India's earliest surviving brick temples; an earlier temple at the site is attributed to Emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE.

source_title: Group of Monuments at Hampi
text: UNESCO identifies the Virupaksha Temple as a sacred component of the Group of Monuments at Hampi. UNESCO describes Hampi as the former capital of the Vijayanagara Empire, with most surviving remains dating from the 14th to 16th centuries, and the property includes sacred, royal and urban remains in the Tungabhadra basin. The UNESCO summary names this temple complex but does not provide a separate construction date or detailed architectural description for it.

source_title: Group of Monuments at Hampi
text: UNESCO identifies the Vitthala Temple Complex as part of the Group of Monuments at Hampi. Its account highlights the complex's Garuda shrine shaped as a granite ratha, along with mandapas, a bazaar street and a stepped tank. UNESCO describes Hampi as the former capital of the Vijayanagara Empire, with most surviving remains dating from the 14th to 16th centuries; it does not assign a separate construction date to this complex in the summary.

source_title: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas
text: The Channakeshava Temple at Belur is a component of UNESCO's Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas, a serial property of 12th- and 13th-century temple complexes. UNESCO describes Hoysala features including stellate plans, circumambulatory platforms, sculptural galleries, tiered friezes and carved chloritic schist. Belur is identified as a living temple with continuing rituals and festivals.

source_title: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas
text: The Hoysalesvara Temple at Halebidu is one of the three components of UNESCO's 12th- and 13th-century Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas. The UNESCO record describes the ensemble's stellate plans, circumambulatory platforms, sculptural galleries, multi-tiered friezes and carved chloritic schist. It notes this temple as a component of a serial heritage property.

source_title: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas
text: The Keshava Temple at Somanathapura is one component of UNESCO's Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas, a serial property dating from the 12th to 13th centuries. UNESCO describes Hoysala architectural characteristics such as stellate plans, sculptural galleries, circumambulatory platforms, multi-tiered friezes and carved chloritic schist.

source_title: Great Living Chola Temples
text: UNESCO states that the Brihadisvara Temple at Gangaikondacholisvaram was built by Rajendra I and completed in 1035. Its vimana is described as 53 metres high. The temple belongs to the Great Living Chola Temples property, whose temples show the development of Chola architecture and art.

source_title: Great Living Chola Temples
text: UNESCO describes the Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram as a Chola temple built by Rajaraja II. Its 24-metre vimana and ornate chariot-like front mandapa are noted in the UNESCO account, along with sculptures associated with Chola art and Saivism. It is one of the three temples in the Great Living Chola Temples property.

source_title: Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple, Telangana
text: UNESCO describes the Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple at Palampet as a 13th-century Kakatiyan temple. Its account highlights the sandbox foundation, lightweight porous bricks in the roof structure, carved stone sculpture and the relation between temple, landscape, ritual and dance traditions. The temple continues ceremonial use.

source_title: Group of Monuments at Pattadakal
text: UNESCO describes Pattadakal as a 7th- and 8th-century Chalukya site where northern and southern Indian architectural forms were brought together. The group contains nine Hindu temples and a Jain sanctuary. The Virupaksha Temple, built around 740 by Queen Lokamahadevi, is highlighted as a major monument in the group.

source_title: Venkataramana Temple, Gingee — Viluppuram District Administration
publisher: Viluppuram District Administration, Government of Tamil Nadu
text: The Viluppuram District Administration describes Gingee's Venkataramana Temple as a Nayaka-period foundation associated with Muthialu Nayaka and dates its construction to 1540–1550. The account notes gopuras and mandapas, sculpted panels depicting episodes from the epics, and Tamil inscriptions. It also records damage and decline following the French occupation after 1761. These details are reported by the district tourism page and remain pending editorial review against the source.

source_title: Mandagapattu — Viluppuram District Administration

The page's chronology is reproduced only as a source-attributed report here; the exact date and interpretation need specialist review. No deity or architectural details beyond those explicitly stated by the source are asserted in this document.

source_title: Indian Archaeology 1975–76: A Review — Panamalai report

text: The Archaeological Survey of India's 1975–76 review reports archaeological work at the Talagirisvara temple at Panamalai, including the removal of later brick accretions that exposed Pallava inscriptions on the temple plinth and vimana. This is a narrowly scoped report of an archaeological observation, not a complete history or conservation assessment. The publication's exact passage and terminology should be checked during human review before this note is treated as settled.

source_title: Kailasanatha Temple, Kanchipuram — Incredible India
publisher: Ministry of Tourism, Government of India
text: The Government of India's Incredible India page dates Kanchipuram's Kailasanatha Temple to around 700 CE and associates its construction with Pallava ruler Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha), with additions attributed to Mahendravarman III. It describes a complex combining rock-cut and structural stone work, a Shiva lingam, subsidiary shrines, a vimana and mandapa with carved reliefs, inscriptions and murals. The page also identifies Maha Shivratri as a significant observance. These are source-reported claims pending human review.

source_title: Archaeological Remains at Srinivasanallur — IGNCA digital library

text: The digitized archaeological publication hosted by the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts discusses the Korangunatha temple at Srinivasanallur and associates it with the reign of Parantaka I (907–955 CE). Its description notes a square vimana, a mandapa, sculptural work and miniature panels; it also remarks on surviving brick fabric in the superstructure. This note is attributed to that publication and requires a page-level editorial check before its architectural and chronological details are treated as verified.

source_title: Sri Vidyashankara Temple — Sringeri Sharada Peetham
text: The Sringeri Sharada Peetham's temple account dates Vidyashankara Temple to 1338 CE and describes its stone construction and combination of Hoysala and Dravidian features. It highlights twelve zodiac-associated pillars and records the Vidyatirtha Rathotsava during Kartika as a seven-day observance. The temple authority also notes the Archaeological Survey of India's role in its care. These statements reflect the cited institution's account and remain pending independent editorial review.

text: Karnataka Tourism describes the Bhoga Nandeeshwara Temple complex at Nandi as an ancient temple complex and gives a ninth-century date in its Nandi Hills visitor overview. This source supports only a concise heritage note; it does not establish detailed construction phases, individual architectural elements, or festival practices for this record. The date and scope are kept attributed to the tourism page and pending review.

source_title: World Heritage Site Nomination Dossier: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (Supplementary Information)
publisher: Government of India / Government of Karnataka, submitted to UNESCO World Heritage Centre
text: The UNESCO-hosted Hoysala temples nomination dossier inventories the Veera Narayana temple at Belavadi, records 1206 CE as its establishment date, and describes it as a living temple under Archaeological Survey of India ownership. The dossier identifies Veera Narayana as the principal shrine and mentions Venu Gopala and Yoga Narasimha subsidiary shrines. Belavadi is documented in a nomination dossier; this source does not mean this individual temple is independently inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List. The dossier's claims remain pending review.

source_title: Badami — Incredible India
publisher: Ministry of Tourism, Government of India
text: The Government of India's Incredible India page describes Badami's cave-temple group as four rock-cut sanctuaries with a hall, pillared veranda and shrine area. Its account identifies Shaiva imagery in Cave 1, Vaishnava imagery in Caves 2 and 3, and a Jain cave (Cave 4), and places the group in the early Chalukya period. This note is limited to the page's broad description; individual dates, iconographic identifications and conservation details require human source review.

source_title: Aihole — Incredible India
publisher: Ministry of Tourism, Government of India
text: The Government of India's Aihole page describes the Durga Temple's distinctive apsidal plan, raised platform and gallery surrounding its sanctum, and notes Archaeological Survey of India conservation. The page presents Aihole as an important early Chalukya temple center. This document records only those broad source-supported points; it does not infer the temple's dedication from its commonly used name. The source and its terminology remain pending editorial review.

source_title: Shree Jagannath Temple
text: The Puri district administration describes the Shree Jagannath Temple as a major place of worship in Puri dedicated to Jagannath, with Balabhadra and Subhadra also central to its worship tradition. The temple is associated with the Eastern Ganga ruler Anantavarman Chodaganga and the 12th-century development of the shrine. Its Kalinga temple complex is closely connected to the annual Rath Yatra, when the deities are carried in processional chariots; the district page also identifies related observances including Snana Yatra and Bahuda Yatra. These notes summarize the administration's visitor information and should be checked against the temple's current ritual calendar before reuse.

source_title: Lingaraj Temple
text: Odisha Tourism presents Lingaraj as an important Bhubaneswar shrine dedicated to Shiva in the Harihara form. Its account places the principal temple in the 11th century and describes a sandstone structure whose tower rises to nearly 180 feet. The complex illustrates the region's Kalinga temple vocabulary, with the principal sanctuary and attached halls forming a large temple precinct. The source notes the self-manifested linga tradition and identifies Maha Shivaratri and Rukuna Ratha Jatra among the temple's important observances. This document records the tourism department's summary; details of construction phases and ritual practice merit specialist review.

source_title: Mukteswara Temple
text: Odisha Tourism dates Mukteswara Temple in Bhubaneswar to around the 10th century and associates it with the Somavamsi ruler Jajati I. The temple is a compact example of Kalinga architecture, organized around a deula (sanctuary tower) and jagamohana (assembly hall). The department highlights the carved arched gateway, sculpted surfaces and perforated lattice windows as distinctive features. The source describes the monument as an important stage in the development of Odisha temple architecture. Its concise account does not establish every attribution or date independently, so those details remain subject to human source review.

source_title: Parsurameswar Temple, Bhubaneswar
text: Odisha Tourism's account identifies Parsurameswar Temple as an early Bhubaneswar monument, generally placed in the 7th century, and dedicated to Shiva. The compact Kalinga shrine combines a sanctuary with an assembly space and is noted for carved figures and panels, including depictions associated with the Saptamatrikas. The temple is useful for understanding early forms of Odisha's stone temple architecture. The date and interpretation here follow the tourism article's summary and should be treated as attributed rather than as a new independent archaeological assessment.

source_title: Ananta Basudeva Temple
text: Odisha Tourism describes Ananta Basudeva Temple in Bhubaneswar as a 13th-century Vaishnava shrine associated with Queen Chandrika Devi of the Eastern Ganga period. Its worship tradition centers on Krishna (Basudeva), with the source also identifying Balarama (Ananta) and Subhadra. The department outlines a multi-part temple complex with a sanctuary, assembly and offering halls. It also notes the temple's association with the preparation and offering of the Mahaprasad tradition known as Abadha. These points are drawn from the tourism authority's overview; ritual details and historical attribution remain pending review.

source_title: Bhaskareswar Temple: monument description
publisher: National Monuments Authority, Government of India
text: The National Monuments Authority's monument description identifies Bhaskareswar as a west-facing Shiva temple with a two-tiered structure and a notably large linga, reported there at about 2.74 metres. The description records a pancharatha ground plan and sculpted niches with figures including Parvati, Kartikeya and Ganesha. It also relays a scholarly proposal that the linga may incorporate a fragment of an Ashokan pillar; this is presented as an attributed hypothesis, not an established fact. The architectural observations in this document are limited to the NMA description and should be checked against the protected-monument record.

source_title: Living Architecture: Indian Temples
publisher: Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (digitized copy from ASI Central Archaeological Library) — Andreas Volwahsen
text: The architectural monograph Living Architecture: Indian Temples discusses the Brahmeswar temple at Bhubaneswar as a Shaiva sanctuary with an assembly hall and four subsidiary shrines in its precinct. Its plates and description show the sanctuary and hall as a coordinated composition, with the hall's pyramidal roof built in receding tiers. The publication illustrates the monument within the mature stone-temple architecture of Odisha. This summary follows the digitized monograph held in the Archaeological Survey of India's Central Archaeological Library; precise construction chronology is not asserted here because the cited excerpt does not establish it.

source_title: Baitala Temple and the Khakhara tradition
publisher: Odisha Review, Government of Odisha (Sujata Routray)
text: An Odisha Review article by Sujata Routray describes Baitala Deula in Bhubaneswar as an 8th-century monument associated with Chamunda worship and the Khakhara form of Kalinga architecture. It distinguishes the sanctuary's elongated, semi-cylindrical roof profile from the more familiar curvilinear temple tower and discusses its sculptural program and tantric associations. These are the article author's historical and architectural interpretations, recorded here with explicit attribution rather than treated as an independent verification. The source is a state-published research article, not a current temple administration page.

source_title: Alampur Nava Brahma Temples
publisher: Jogulamba Gadwal District Administration, Government of Telangana
text: The Jogulamba Gadwal district administration presents Alampur's Nava Brahma group as nine Shiva shrines associated with the Badami Chalukya period, broadly the 6th–7th centuries. The temples are distinguished by individual names and architectural forms within a shared sacred landscape; the district source identifies Bala Brahma as the principal shrine and notes its continuing worship. The complex demonstrates early Deccan temple building and the region's historical connections. The administration page includes dates and local traditions that require monument-level corroboration; this draft retains only its group-level account and does not assign the same detailed history to every shrine.

source_title: Thousand Pillars Temple
text: Telangana Tourism dates the Thousand Pillars Temple at Hanamkonda to 1163 and associates its construction with Kakatiya ruler Rudra Deva. The department describes a shrine tradition honoring Shiva, Vishnu and Surya and highlights the star-shaped plan, carved pillars and monolithic Nandi. The building is presented as an example of Kakatiya-era craftsmanship, with the sculpted stone supports giving the monument its familiar name. These claims follow the state tourism page; architectural dating and conservation status should be checked against the responsible archaeology authority before being treated as fully verified.

source_title: Lepakshi Veerabhadra Temple
publisher: Sri Sathya Sai District Administration, Government of Andhra Pradesh
text: The Sri Sathya Sai district tourism page identifies the Veerabhadra Temple at Lepakshi as a Vijayanagara-period complex and points visitors to its sculptural and architectural features, including the celebrated hanging pillar. The complex includes shrines associated with Veerabhadra and other Hindu deities. The district account also preserves the local association of the site with the Vijayanagara official Virupanna; this is recorded as the administration's account, not expanded into unsupported legend. The page is a general tourism overview, so individual construction dates, mural descriptions and conservation interventions require stronger monument-specific sourcing.

source_title: Chintala Venkataramana Swamy Temple
publisher: Ananthapuramu District Administration, Government of Andhra Pradesh
text: The Ananthapuramu district administration identifies the Tadipatri shrine as Chintala Venkataramana Swamy Temple, also called Chintalarayaswami, and describes it as a temple to Vishnu in the Venkateswara form. Its page associates construction in the 16th century with Pemmasani Timmanayudu II under Vijayanagara rule, and notes the gopuram and carved mandapa. Vaikuntha Ekadashi and Brahmotsavam are listed among its observances. These details are transcribed in paraphrase from the district's temple page; current festival schedules and the exact chronology remain for review.

source_title: Indian Archaeology 2012–13: A Review
publisher: Archaeological Survey of India, National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities digital archive
text: The Archaeological Survey of India's 2012–13 annual review records conservation work at the Madhavaraya temple in Gorantla: exposed flooring members were addressed with granite flooring laid over lime concrete, with slopes and drainage channels provided. This is a specific conservation record for the reported work period, not a description of the temple's complete history or its present condition. No further historical or architectural claims are included because this source excerpt is focused on conservation.

source_title: Gwalior
publisher: Incredible India, Ministry of Tourism, Government of India
text: The Government of India's Incredible India Gwalior guide describes the Sas Bahu temples within Gwalior Fort as a pair of historic shrines, one associated with Vishnu and the other with Shiva, and highlights their carved stone surfaces. The twin monuments are commonly dated to the 11th century in the guide's historical overview. Their contrasting scale and detailed exterior carving make them notable examples of the region's medieval temple architecture. This draft deliberately follows the national tourism summary and does not expand the popular name into an unsupported personal story.

source_title: Great Living Chola Temples
text: UNESCO's Great Living Chola Temples property includes Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram alongside the major Chola temples at Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram. UNESCO describes Airavatesvara as a 12th-century monument commissioned under Rajaraja II, notable for its sculpted stone architecture and a chariot-form mandapa. The property is recognized for its outstanding Chola temple architecture and continuing religious use. UNESCO's page identifies the Archaeological Survey of India as responsible for protection and conservation of the centrally protected monuments, while worship and temple administration involve the relevant local authority. This is a property-level heritage summary, not a detailed conservation-condition assessment of Airavatesvara alone.

source_title: Aihole
publisher: Incredible India, Ministry of Tourism, Government of India
text: The Government of India's Aihole guide describes Lad Khan Temple as an early Chalukya-period monument with a hall-like, panchayat-style plan and a shrine dedicated to Shiva. Its form differs from the later, more familiar towering temple compositions and is useful for tracing experiments in early Deccan temple architecture. The guide explains that the name Lad Khan is connected to a later occupant rather than the original temple dedication. This account is attributed to the tourism source; the monument's more precise date and construction sequence are not asserted here.

source_title: Mallikarjuna Temple, Pattadakal
text: Karnataka Tourism associates the Mallikarjuna Temple at Pattadakal with Queen Trailokyamahadevi and the 8th-century Chalukya period, linking its construction to the political context of Vikramaditya II's campaigns against the Pallavas. The temple is dedicated to Shiva and is described with a southern-style pyramidal tower, pillared mandapa and sculptural panels drawing on epic narratives. It stands within Pattadakal, the UNESCO-listed group of Chalukya monuments. This document distinguishes the state tourism account's historical interpretation from independently reviewed epigraphic evidence.

source_title: Karnataka Tourist Guide
text: The Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation guide places Papanatha Temple within the UNESCO World Heritage monuments of Pattadakal. It draws attention to the temple's richly carved surfaces, decorated ceilings and a substantial pillared main hall. These features form part of the mixed architectural landscape at Pattadakal, where temple forms reflect the Chalukya period's interaction of northern and southern design vocabularies. This short document is limited to architectural details given in the tourism guide; it does not add a precise construction date or deity claim beyond what is established in the existing catalogue.

source_title: Hoysala Temples of Belur, Halebidu and Somnathapura: ICOMOS evaluation
text: The ICOMOS evaluation dossier for the Hoysala temples describes the Halebidu Hoysalesvara monument as a double-shrine temple dedicated to Shiva, with paired sanctums, associated Nandi pavilions, star-shaped plans and an extensive narrative sculptural frieze around the platform. The dossier discusses the site within the Hoysala architectural tradition and records its role in the historic Hoysala capital. Its conservation discussion describes the protected monument and preservation context. These details come from the advisory evaluation for UNESCO nomination and should be cited as an institutional assessment, not as a current conservation inspection.

source_title: Hoysala Temples of Belur, Halebidu and Somnathapura: ICOMOS evaluation
text: The ICOMOS evaluation describes the Keshava Temple at Somanathapura as a late major Hoysala temple, consecrated in 1268 under the patronage of Somanatha Dandanayaka. Its plan has three sanctums arranged around a shared hall, with stellate outlines and sculpted exterior bands; the three shrines are associated with forms of Vishnu. The dossier also documents the temple's inclusion in the Hoysala temple serial property inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2023. These claims follow the UNESCO nomination evaluation and are kept specific to the Somanathapura monument.

title: Mahabodhi: historical and religious setting
source_title: Mahabodhi Temple Complex at Bodh Gaya
text: UNESCO identifies Bodh Gaya as one of four holy sites associated with the life of the Buddha, particularly his enlightenment. It records an earliest temple commissioned by Emperor Asoka in the 3rd century BCE and dates the present temple to the 5th–6th centuries CE. The complex also preserves evidence of worship and sanctuary-building over a long period. These statements describe the UNESCO property and its documented history; they do not establish details of every later ritual.

title: Mahabodhi: temple form and sacred precinct
source_title: Mahabodhi Temple Complex at Bodh Gaya
text: UNESCO describes the present main temple as an early surviving brick Buddhist temple of the late Gupta period. Its account identifies a roughly 50-metre temple, the Vajrasana and sacred Bodhi Tree, six other sacred sites associated with enlightenment, and ancient votive stupas within the protected enclosure; the Lotus Pond lies outside the enclosure to the south. It also describes a curvilinear tower, or shikhara, with an amalaka and kalasha, and Buddha images in niches. This architectural summary follows UNESCO's description of the listed complex.

title: Khajuraho: Chandella period and Nagara design
source_title: Khajuraho Group of Monuments
text: UNESCO presents Khajuraho as a culmination of northern Indian temple art under the Chandella rulers of the 10th and 11th centuries CE. The listed group comprises 23 temples, including one partly excavated structure, in western, eastern and southern clusters. UNESCO describes the temples as sandstone buildings on ornate raised platforms, with a sanctum tower and subsidiary miniature spires characteristic of the Nagara form. The plan moves through porch, hall, vestibule and sanctum, with circumambulatory paths in some examples.

title: Khajuraho: sculptural programme and protection
source_title: Khajuraho Group of Monuments
text: UNESCO describes sculpture as integrated with Khajuraho's architecture: carved surfaces include sacred and secular motifs, worship, deities, domestic life, teachers, dancers and musicians. The UNESCO record states that the property was inscribed in 1986. It identifies Government of India ownership and Archaeological Survey of India management under the national monuments legislation, with regulated and prohibited zones around designated monuments. These are property-level heritage and management facts, not a claim that every individual temple has the same sculptures or conservation condition.

title: Virupaksha at Hampi: expansion and living worship
source_title: Section II: Periodic Report on the State of Conservation of the Group of Monuments at Hampi, India, 2003
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre / Archaeological Survey of India report
text: The UNESCO/ASI periodic report describes Virupaksha, also called Pampapati, as Hampi's most sacred living monument. It says the complex began as a small shrine and expanded to its present dimensions in the first half of the 16th century. The report describes two large courts within a rectangular enclosure, towered gateways, and a sequence of sanctum, vestibule, ardha-mantapa and large maha-mantapa. It records that Krishnadevaraya built the smaller eastern gopura and painted pillared ranga-mantapa in 1510, and identifies the sanctum image as a Shiva linga called Virupaksha. The ceiling paintings in the ranga-mantapa are identified as Vijayanagara-period.

title: Vitthala at Hampi: Vijayanagara expansion and plan
source_title: Section II: Periodic Report on the State of Conservation of the Group of Monuments at Hampi, India, 2003
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre / Archaeological Survey of India report
text: The UNESCO/ASI periodic report calls the Vitthala complex a high point of Vijayanagara art and architecture. It records that a core existed in the reign of Devaraya II (1422–1446) and that Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529) made substantial additions. The described complex includes a main shrine for Vitthala, a devi shrine, kalyana-mantapa, utsava-mantapa, a hundred-pillared mantapa and the stone chariot. The main shrine plan includes sanctum, vestibule, a closed circumambulatory path, open maha-mantapa and ardha-mantapa.

title: Vitthala at Hampi: carved pillars and documented conservation
source_title: Section II: Periodic Report on the State of Conservation of the Group of Monuments at Hampi, India, 2003
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre / Archaeological Survey of India report
text: The UNESCO/ASI report describes the Vitthala assembly hall's composite granite pillars with rearing animals and riders, and clusters of slender subsidiary pillars. It notes that gently tapped small pillars produce musical notes. In its 2003 conservation account, the report documents structural work at the Vitthala entrance and shrine, including strengthening broken lintel and beams and stabilizing masonry at the gopura. This is a dated record of work reported in 2003, not a statement of present condition.

title: Achyutaraya at Hampi: patronage, plan and bazaar
source_title: Section II: Periodic Report on the State of Conservation of the Group of Monuments at Hampi, India, 2003
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre / Archaeological Survey of India report
text: The UNESCO/ASI periodic report dates the Achyutaraya (Tiruvengalanatha) temple to 1534 and attributes its construction to Hiriya Tirumalaraja Wodeyar, a mahamandaleshwara serving under Achutadevaraya. It describes a north-facing temple within a double enclosure, a spacious courtyard, and a long bazaar called Achyutarayapete. The report gives the inner plan as sanctum, vestibule, ardha-mantapa and ornate maha-mantapa. It also records an inscriptional reference to a weekly Tuesday market; this is evidence reported in the source, not a claim about present market activity.

title: Gangaikondacholapuram: Rajendra I and Chola architecture
source_title: Great Living Chola Temples
text: UNESCO states that Rajendra I (1012–1044 CE) built the Brihadisvara temple at Gangaikondacholapuram for Shiva. It describes exceptional sculpture and identifies the bronzes of Bhogasakti and Subrahmanya as notable Chola metal icons. UNESCO places the temple within the Great Living Chola Temples property and regards the three temples at Thanjavur, Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram as outstanding evidence of Chola architecture and ideology. The source does not establish details of current festival schedules.

title: Brihadisvara at Thanjavur: Dravida form and Chola heritage
source_title: Great Living Chola Temples
text: UNESCO describes the Thanjavur Brihadisvara as the first great example in the development represented by the Great Living Chola Temples, an outstanding creative achievement in the pure Dravida form. The property is recognized as testimony to the development of Chola architecture and Tamil civilization. This document adds UNESCO's property-level architectural and heritage framing; it does not repeat unverified construction measurements from secondary sources.

title: Shore Temple: structural Pallava architecture at Mahabalipuram
source_title: Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram
text: UNESCO situates the Shore Temple within the Pallava monument group at Mahabalipuram, created by a dynasty that ruled the area from the 6th to 9th centuries CE. The group includes rock-cut caves, monolithic temples, reliefs, structural temples and excavated remains. UNESCO describes the Shore Temple as the culmination of structural monuments at the site and notes its Dravida vimana layout along the sea. This source supports the Shore Temple's place in the Pallava architectural sequence; it does not assign every feature of the broader group to this temple.

title: Meenakshi-Sundareswarar: twin shrines and urban growth
source_title: Sri Meenakshi - Sundareswarar Temple
publisher: Madurai District Administration, Government of Tamil Nadu
text: Madurai District Administration describes Meenakshi and Sundareswarar as the paired deities of the twin-temple complex and says the city developed around it. The district account attributes the complex's growth to successive dynasties and monarchs, and identifies substantial expansion under Thirumalai Nayak (1623–1655 CE). It describes five gateways enclosing the two shrines and highlights the Ayiramkaal Mandapam, or Hall of Thousand Pillars, and stone musical pillars. These are claims in the district tourism account and are retained for human review.

title: Madurai temple traditions in the district festival account
source_title: Festivals and Events
publisher: Madurai District Administration, Government of Tamil Nadu
text: The Madurai District Administration festival page describes the Chithirai festival, held in April or May, in connection with the marriage of Meenakshi and Sundareswarar and Alagar's journey toward Madurai. The page also lists the cradle festival and Avanimoolam among Madurai's religious events. This is the district's description of local tradition; its mythic narrative is presented as religious tradition rather than independently verifiable historical fact. The page does not provide a current-year schedule.

title: Kashi Vishvanath: Shiva worship and Jyotirlinga tradition
source_title: Shree Kashi Vishvanath Temple
publisher: Varanasi District Administration, Government of Uttar Pradesh
text: The Varanasi District Administration identifies Kashi Vishvanath as a Hindu temple dedicated to Shiva on the western bank of the Ganga in Varanasi. It identifies the main deity as Vishvanatha or Vishveshvara and describes the temple as one of the twelve Jyotirlingas. The page explains that the name Kashi is also used for Varanasi. This document covers the district source's religious and location description only; detailed construction history and festival practices remain research gaps.

title: Konark: 13th-century Surya sanctuary and historical setting
source_title: Sun Temple, Konârak
text: UNESCO dates the Sun Temple at Konârak to the 13th century and frames it as an outstanding testimony to the 13th-century kingdom of Orissa. The UNESCO account connects the monument to the spread of Surya worship to eastern India. It also records an inscribed property of 10.62 hectares in Puri District and an inscription date of 1984. The page separately recounts a dramatic construction story involving a master builder and his son; that account is presented there as legend, not as established construction history, and is not used here as fact.

title: Konark: the solar chariot and surviving temple spaces
source_title: Sun Temple, Konârak
text: UNESCO describes the monument as a monumental representation of Surya's chariot, with 24 decorated wheels and a team of six horses. Its architectural account identifies the surviving Jagamohana (audience hall) and the temple's sculptural integration with the built form; the principal sanctuary tower (vimana) no longer survives. This profile distinguishes surviving fabric from the larger original conception and does not assume that every element remains intact.

title: Konark: sculpture as architecture and narrative
source_title: Sun Temple, Konârak
text: UNESCO treats Konark's sculpture and architecture as an integrated artistic programme: sculptural relief is part of the monument's form, design and narrative effect. The property retains surviving structures and sculptures as well as displaced remains preserved in situ. UNESCO also associates the site's cultural continuity with living practices, including the Chandrabhaga festival. This source does not provide a current festival calendar, ritual sequence or event schedule.

title: Konark: heritage status, protection and conservation concerns
source_title: Sun Temple, Konârak
text: The Sun Temple at Konârak was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1984. UNESCO states that it is protected under India's Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains framework and that conservation programmes are undertaken by the Archaeological Survey of India. Its property record identifies historical structural concerns and environmental pressures, and calls for continuing structural and material conservation of the Jagamohana and sculptures. These are the concerns recorded on the UNESCO page; they should not be read as a real-time condition assessment.

title: Ramappa: Kakatiya period, patrons and construction chronology
source_title: Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple, Telangana
text: UNESCO places Rudreshwara, popularly called Ramappa, within the Kakatiya period (1123–1323 CE) and associates the walled complex with rulers Rudradeva and Recharla Rudra. It dates the beginning of the sandstone temple's construction to 1213 CE and says work is believed to have continued for about four decades. The source names the principal shrine as a Shiva temple. These are UNESCO's documented chronology and attribution; the document does not infer a precise completion year.

title: Ramappa: materials, vimana and construction engineering
source_title: Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple, Telangana
text: UNESCO describes sandstone construction, decorated beams and pillars carved from granite and dolerite, and a distinctive pyramidal, horizontally stepped vimana. Its roof structure uses lightweight porous bricks, popularly called floating bricks, to reduce weight. The UNESCO Outstanding Universal Value account also describes experimentation with a sandbox foundation and material selection as part of the site's engineering significance. The terms here follow UNESCO's interpretation and do not claim that a single technique alone explains the temple's structural performance.

title: Ramappa: bracket figures, stone carving and dance imagery
source_title: Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple, Telangana
text: UNESCO highlights the temple's hard dolerite carvings, especially bracket figures, for their finely worked surfaces and sense of movement. The sculptural programme depicts regional dance customs and Kakatiya cultural forms, including figures and motifs identified in UNESCO's evaluation. Rather than treating these images as a complete record of historical dance, this profile describes them as visual evidence interpreted by UNESCO as expressing local artistic and cultural traditions.

title: Ramappa: World Heritage recognition, landscape and living practice
source_title: Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple, Telangana
text: The Kakatiya Rudreshwara Temple was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2021. UNESCO presents its heritage value through the relationship among temple architecture, sculpture, ritual, dance and the surrounding landscape, including agricultural land and the Kakatiya-built Ramappa Cheruvu reservoir. UNESCO also describes the complex as a living Shaiva temple where ceremonies continue. The page says the Archaeological Survey of India has maintained and conserved the protected monument since its identification as protected in 1914; this is the source's account, not an independent condition audit.

title: Pattadakal Virupaksha: Chalukya-era patronage
source_title: Group of Monuments at Pattadakal
text: UNESCO places the Virupaksha Temple within the 7th- and 8th-century Chalukya monuments at Pattadakal. It dates the temple to about 740 CE and attributes its construction to Queen Lokamahadevi, who commissioned it to commemorate her husband's victory over southern rulers. The source describes Virupaksha as a prominent monument within the wider group; this short chronology is based on UNESCO's group record and does not add a more precise building sequence.

title: Pattadakal Virupaksha: architectural setting within the monument group
source_title: Group of Monuments at Pattadakal
text: UNESCO characterizes Pattadakal as an eclectic artistic centre where architectural forms associated with northern and southern India were brought into a harmonious blend under Chalukya patronage. The property includes a series of nine Hindu temples and a Jain sanctuary, with Virupaksha singled out as a masterpiece. The description is group-level: it supports the temple's place in Pattadakal's architectural setting, but does not assign every stylistic feature of all ten monuments to Virupaksha alone.

title: Krishna Temple at Hampi: foundation and royal context
source_title: Section II: Periodic Report on the State of Conservation of the Group of Monuments at Hampi, India, 2003
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre / Archaeological Survey of India report
text: The 2003 UNESCO/ASI periodic report dates the Krishna Temple to 1513 and associates its construction with Vijayanagara ruler Krishnadevaraya. The report notes an inscribed account that the Balakrishna image enshrined at the temple had been brought from Udayagiri in present-day Odisha. This document reports what the historical conservation dossier records; it does not infer that the present image or all current worship practices are unchanged from the period described.

title: Krishna Temple at Hampi: shrine sequence and subsidiary spaces
source_title: Section II: Periodic Report on the State of Conservation of the Group of Monuments at Hampi, India, 2003
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre / Archaeological Survey of India report
text: The 2003 UNESCO/ASI report describes a temple sequence comprising sanctum, vestibule, circumambulatory passage, maha-mantapa and ardha-mantapa. It also records a Devi shrine to the north and a sacred tank within the complex. The description is useful for understanding the plan documented by the report, while its date means that present access, condition and management should be checked separately.

title: Krishna Temple at Hampi: inscriptions and the associated market
source_title: Section II: Periodic Report on the State of Conservation of the Group of Monuments at Hampi, India, 2003
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre / Archaeological Survey of India report
text: The 2003 UNESCO/ASI report links the Krishna Temple to an inscription about the installation of the Balakrishna image and records a bazaar beside the temple, including references to market activity in the historical urban setting. The document preserves the report's evidence about the relationship between a sacred complex and commercial space at Hampi. It does not claim that the historical market continues today.

title: Pattabhirama Temple at Hampi: date and historical setting
source_title: Section II: Periodic Report on the State of Conservation of the Group of Monuments at Hampi, India, 2003
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre / Archaeological Survey of India report
text: The UNESCO/ASI periodic report describes Pattabhirama as a 16th-century Vijayanagara temple complex and identifies it as one of the largest temple enclosures at Hampi. Its account places the temple in the wider sacred and urban landscape of the Vijayanagara capital. This is a period attribution from a 2003 conservation report; it does not establish a precise foundation year or identify a named patron where the cited passage does not do so.

title: Pattabhirama Temple at Hampi: courtyard and pillared halls
source_title: Section II: Periodic Report on the State of Conservation of the Group of Monuments at Hampi, India, 2003
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre / Archaeological Survey of India report
text: The 2003 UNESCO/ASI report describes Pattabhirama's spacious courtyard, eastern tower, large pillared halls and kalyana-mantapa. It places these halls within a large Vijayanagara-period enclosure, whose scale and open courtyard distinguish the complex's overall plan in the report. These features form the basis of this profile's architectural account. The report describes the complex as a whole and the document avoids claiming a specific ritual use for every hall unless the report names it. The source does not establish that all structures have remained in the same condition since the survey.

title: Pattabhirama Temple at Hampi: conservation recorded in 2003
source_title: Section II: Periodic Report on the State of Conservation of the Group of Monuments at Hampi, India, 2003
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre / Archaeological Survey of India report
text: In its 2003 conservation account, the UNESCO/ASI report records work at Pattabhirama that included floor pointing, roof water-tightening, replacement of broken beams in the maha-mantapa, work on the circumambulatory-path floor, and repairs to navaranga pillars and beams. These are dated interventions documented in 2003. They should not be interpreted as a report of current structural condition or as evidence that the same work remains adequate today.

title: Hemakuta at Hampi: an early and long-lived sacred landscape
source_title: Section II: Periodic Report on the State of Conservation of the Group of Monuments at Hampi, India, 2003
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre / Archaeological Survey of India report
text: The 2003 UNESCO/ASI periodic report describes Hemakuta as a group that includes temples spanning approximately the 9th through 16th centuries, with parts of the sacred landscape predating the main Vijayanagara urban phase. The report identifies the group as a large complex with substantial boundary walls and gateways. It therefore should not be assigned a single construction date or treated as one uniform building campaign.

title: Hemakuta at Hampi: temple forms and the Prasanna Virupaksha shrine
source_title: Section II: Periodic Report on the State of Conservation of the Group of Monuments at Hampi, India, 2003
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre / Archaeological Survey of India report
text: The 2003 UNESCO/ASI report notes single-, double- and triple-celled temple plans within the Hemakuta group. It identifies the Prasanna Virupaksha shrine as having a Kadamba-Nagara superstructure and records a date of 1338 for that shrine. These architectural and dating details apply to the named component and typologies described in the report, not automatically to every Hemakuta structure.

temple_name: Sun temple, Surya kind with adjoining other temples and loose sculptures
title: Modhera Sun Temple: historical attribution and solar dedication
source_title: Sun Temple, Modhera and its adjoining monuments
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre; nomination submitted by India
text: The Indian State Party's UNESCO Tentative List nomination presents Modhera as a Surya temple and places it within Gujarat's Solanki-period architectural heritage. The nomination associates its style with the 11th-century Maru-Gurjara tradition and discusses Bhima I as the historical context; its dating is stylistic rather than a securely stated construction year. Because the page is a national nomination, its claims are attributed to that submission. Modhera is on UNESCO's Tentative List, not the World Heritage List.

temple_name: Sun temple, Surya kind with adjoining other temples and loose sculptures
title: Modhera Sun Temple: shrine, assembly hall and sacred tank
source_title: Sun Temple, Modhera and its adjoining monuments
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre; nomination submitted by India
text: The Tentative List nomination describes an ensemble of a principal shrine with a gudhamandapa, a separate Sabhamandapa or assembly hall, and a sacred tank called Ramakunda or Suryakunda in the same account. The buildings sit on a paved platform, with the hall distinct from the main shrine and the tank in front. The description records an east-facing layout and yellow sandstone. This profile follows the nomination and does not imply that every part survives in its original complete form.

temple_name: Sun temple, Surya kind with adjoining other temples and loose sculptures
title: Modhera Sun Temple: Surya imagery and carved architectural surfaces
source_title: Sun Temple, Modhera and its adjoining monuments
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre; nomination submitted by India
text: The Indian nomination describes Surya figures as prominent in the temple's sculptural scheme, including figures placed in niches around the circumambulatory passage and on shrine walls. It also records deities, dancers and narrative imagery across architectural surfaces, with the twelve Adityas among the named iconographic groups. The page describes the Sabhamandapa as an open pillared hall with an octagonal central arrangement and carved surfaces. These claims are attributed to India's Tentative List submission.
