source_title: Sun Temple, Modhera and its adjoining monuments
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre; nomination submitted by India
text: India submitted the Modhera and adjoining monuments property to UNESCO's Tentative List in December 2022. This is a nomination status, not World Heritage inscription. The nomination says the Archaeological Survey of India is responsible for conservation and describes protected areas under India's monuments framework. Those statements reflect the submitted nomination; this document does not provide a current condition survey, visitor timetable or a dated inventory of recent conservation work.

title: Vaikuntaperumal: Pallava patronage and Kanchipuram context
source_title: Temples of Kanchipuram
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre; nomination submitted by India
text: The Indian nomination for the Temples of Kanchipuram identifies Paramesvara Vinnagaram, also called Vaikuntaperumal, as one of the city's nominated monuments. It places the shrine in Pallava Kanchipuram and associates its construction with Pallava ruler Nandivarman II Pallavamalla (731–796 CE). The same submission describes Kanchipuram as a major religious and political centre that later remained important under the Cholas. The city-wide context is not specific to this temple alone.

title: Vaikuntaperumal: stacked sanctums and architectural plan
source_title: Temples of Kanchipuram
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre; nomination submitted by India
text: The Kanchipuram nomination describes Vaikuntaperumal's unusual three-level shrine arrangement, with Vishnu shown in seated, reclining and standing forms on successive levels. It calls the vimana an ashtanga form and describes a surrounding mandapa and sculptural cloister. These details come from the Indian Tentative List account. The source does not provide a current access guide to the upper levels, so the document makes no claim about visitor access.

title: Vaikuntaperumal: cloister reliefs and Pallava inscriptions
source_title: Temples of Kanchipuram
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre; nomination submitted by India
text: The nomination describes narrative reliefs along the inner cloister that present a sequence associated with the Pallava dynasty. It notes that captions or labels carved with the panels help identify figures and events, and records Pallava inscriptions associated with the temple, including an early inscription from the reign of Nandivarman II. The nomination also reports later grants connected to Vaishnava worship. Its dynastic visual narrative includes legendary ancestry; the reliefs should not be treated by themselves as independent proof of every genealogical claim.

title: Vaikuntaperumal: Vaishnava worship and tentative heritage status
source_title: Temples of Kanchipuram
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre; nomination submitted by India
text: The Kanchipuram nomination includes Vaikuntaperumal among the city's important Vaishnava temples and notes that several Vishnu shrines in Kanchipuram were praised by Alvar saints. Its temple-specific discussion associates the shrine with the Vaishnava tradition, while the city's broader religious history is shared by Shaiva, Vaishnava, Buddhist and Jain communities. The group of Kanchipuram temples is on UNESCO's Tentative List; it is not an inscribed World Heritage property. The nomination does not establish the temple's current festival calendar.

title: Baijnath: foundation recorded in Sanskrit inscriptions
source_title: 100 Temples of Baijnath and Sidhnath (Baijnath)
publisher: Archaeological Survey of India; digitized by Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts
text: The Archaeological Survey of India inventory describes two extensive Sarada-script inscriptions, composed in Sanskrit verse, that refer to the temple's construction around 1204 CE by two wealthy merchants from Kiragrama. The inventory identifies the shrine with Shiva Vaidyanatha and describes it as an important sacred monument of the Beas valley. The Kangra district administration separately says the present shrine replaced an earlier Shiva temple on the spot. The surviving inscriptional evidence supports the present temple's medieval foundation; it does not establish the date of the earlier shrine.

title: Baijnath: Nagara shikhara, mandapa and sculptural imagery
source_title: 100 Temples of Baijnath and Sidhnath (Baijnath)
publisher: Archaeological Survey of India; digitized by Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts
text: The ASI inventory describes a sanctum surmounted by a Nagara-style shikhara, a front mandapa with a low pyramidal roof, and a porch. It records a Nandi figure beneath a canopy supported by four stone pillars. The inventory also names sculptures of Shiva-Gangadhara, Ganesha, Karttikeya and Bhairava. These details are specific to the main Baijnath temple and come from the ASI's monument description.

title: Baijnath: Shiva worship and continuing religious use
source_title: Kangra Pilgrimage
publisher: Kangra District Administration, Government of Himachal Pradesh
text: The Kangra District Administration states that the Baijnath temple has remained under worship since its construction in 1204 CE. It describes the sanctum's self-manifested Shiva linga, the vestibule and square mandapa, balconies to the north and south, and Nandi shrine at the porch. The district page reflects the local religious description of the linga as svayambhu and does not provide a current festival schedule. The source's present-tense account was accessed on 2026-11-05.

title: Martand Sun Temple: Lalitaditya-era attribution
source_title: Martand Temple (National Monuments Authority meeting record, 254th meeting)
publisher: National Monuments Authority, Ministry of Culture, Government of India
text: A monument description reproduced by India's National Monuments Authority attributes Martand Sun Temple to Lalitaditya (724–761 CE). It locates the ruins in Anantnag District near Mattan. This is a government monument summary, rather than an inscription transcription or a full archaeological report; the attribution is therefore preserved as the NMA's stated account. A historical claim in the same summary about the temple's destruction is disputed in scholarship and has been omitted from this profile.

title: Martand: courtyard plan, shrine sequence and sculptural niches
source_title: Martand Temple (National Monuments Authority meeting record, 254th meeting)
publisher: National Monuments Authority, Ministry of Culture, Government of India
text: The National Monuments Authority description says the temple stands on a high plinth within a rectangular courtyard lined by cells and faces west. It describes a main shrine sequence of sanctum, vestibule and mandapa approached by a monumental stair. The platform niches are said to contain images including Surya, Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva, Parvati, Ganga, Yamuna and directional deities. The source describes the monument as largely ruined; this profile does not infer the original roof or details that no longer survive.

title: Martand: location and limits of available visitor information
source_title: Martand Sun Temple
publisher: Anantnag District Administration, Government of Jammu and Kashmir
text: The Anantnag District Administration identifies Martand as a tourist place in Anantnag District and describes its setting as a ruin of the Sun Temple. The district page is useful for broad location and visitor orientation, but does not establish current opening hours, access restrictions, services or conservation condition. Visitors should check current local notices before travel; this statement is a limit of the available source rather than an itinerary or access guarantee.

title: Brihadisvara at Thanjavur: court, sanctum and dance imagery in the UNESCO account
source_title: Great Living Chola Temples
text: UNESCO's Great Living Chola Temples property description gives a more detailed architectural account of Brihadisvara at Thanjavur. It places the sanctum in the rear half of a rectangular court enclosed by a large colonnaded prakara, with sub-shrines for the ashtadikpalas and an entrance gopura called Rajarajantiruvasal. The page describes a circumambulatory passage around the sanctum and reports that 81 of the 108 karanas are carved on the second bhumi around the garbhagriha. It also identifies mural paintings and an Amman shrine dated approximately to the 13th century. The source gives a vimana height of 59.82 metres; this differs from an approximately 66-metre figure in other corpus material, so the measurement should be checked by a human reviewer before the records are reconciled.

title: Gangaikondacholisvaram: planned shrines and later additions
source_title: Great Living Chola Temples
text: UNESCO's account of the Great Living Chola Temples distinguishes the original planned components at Gangaikondacholisvaram from later additions. It identifies the Chandesa and Amman sub-shrines and the Simhakeni, or lion well, as features belonging to Rajendra I's plan; it also lists Thenkailasha, Ganesha and Durga shrines as additions made over time. UNESCO presents those later additions as compatible with the continuing life of a worshipping temple, rather than as evidence that the complex remained unchanged. This is a summary of the UNESCO property description, not an independent inscriptional analysis.

title: Airavatesvara: chariot-form mandapa and Nayanmar friezes
source_title: Great Living Chola Temples
text: UNESCO describes Airavatesvara at Darasuram as a complex with a sanctum that has no circumambulatory path and with axial mandapas. Its front mandapa is identified in inscriptions as Rajagambhiran tirumandapam and is conceived as a chariot with wheels. UNESCO notes the ornate pillars and sculpture-dominated elevations, and singles out labelled miniature friezes depicting episodes associated with the 63 Nayanmars, or Saiva saints. The description also records a separate Deivanayaki Amman shrine built slightly later than the main temple. These details are specific to the Darasuram component of the World Heritage property.

title: Mahabodhi: documented restoration history and management framework
source_title: Mahabodhi Temple Complex at Bodh Gaya
text: The UNESCO property account describes the Mahabodhi complex as having components from different periods. It records the main temple as dating broadly to the 5th–6th centuries CE, followed by repairs and renovations, a long period of abandonment described as spanning the 13th–18th centuries, extensive restoration in the 19th century and further work in the second half of the 20th century. UNESCO identifies the State Government of Bihar and the Bodhgaya Temple Management Committee as responsible for management under the Bodh Gaya Temple Act of 1949, and says conservation and restoration work is undertaken with expert guidance from the Archaeological Survey of India. This is the dated historical account presented by the source; it is not a report of present-day condition.

title: Shore Temple in the Pallava sequence of rock-cut and structural monuments
source_title: Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram
text: UNESCO places the Shore Temple within the wider Pallava monument group at Mahabalipuram and describes it as the culmination of the site's structural temple building. The same account distinguishes rock-cut cave mandapas, monolithic rathas carved from large boulders, open-air reliefs and structural temples, presenting these as different stages and forms of Pallava architectural work rather than as parts of the Shore Temple alone. UNESCO also records excavated remains around the Shore Temple, including a stepped structure, miniature shrine, Bhuvaraha image, reclining Vishnu image and a well carved from bedrock, which it associates with the reign of Narasimhavarman Rajasimha (638–660 CE). These are site-group findings and should not be confused with features inside the Shore Temple itself.

title: Hoysalesvara at Halebidu: worship status recorded in UNESCO's 2023 nomination decision
source_title: Decision 45 COM 8B.38 — Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas
text: UNESCO's 2023 decision for the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas describes worship at Hoysalesvara Temple, Halebidu, as long discontinued. It says only symbolic worship is permitted and that rituals and festivals are not allowed. This is a statement in the nomination-era UNESCO record, not a live access notice; present rules should be checked with the responsible authorities. The same decision identifies Hoysalesvara as one of three components of the inscribed serial property, alongside Belur and Somanathapura.

title: Keshava at Somanathapura: UNESCO record of non-worshipping use
source_title: Decision 45 COM 8B.38 — Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas
text: UNESCO's 2023 decision identifies Keshava Temple at Somanathapura as one of the three component monuments of the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas and describes it as a non-worshipping temple. The statement concerns the temple's use as recorded for the World Heritage nomination; it does not establish current visitor hours, admission rules or access arrangements.

title: Halebidu within the 2025 UNESCO conservation decision for the Hoysala ensembles
source_title: Decision 47 COM 7B.73 — Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas
text: In its 2025 decision on the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas, the World Heritage Committee notes progress in community involvement and conservation around the Belur component and records the State Party's commitment to monitor air-pollution impacts on sculptures across the serial property's components. The decision encourages mitigation based on monitoring outcomes and requests an updated state-of-conservation report by 1 December 2026. These are group-level management observations and a dated committee request, not a current condition assessment specific to every Hoysalesvara sculpture.

title: Somanathapura within the 2025 UNESCO conservation decision for the Hoysala ensembles
source_title: Decision 47 COM 7B.73 — Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas
text: The 2025 UNESCO World Heritage Committee decision treats Keshava Temple at Somanathapura as a component of the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas and encourages monitoring and mitigation of air-pollution impacts on the serial property's sculptures. It also records progress at Belur and asks the State Party for an updated conservation report by 1 December 2026. The Belur-specific progress statements should not be transferred to Somanathapura; only the serial-property monitoring request applies here.

title: Shree Jagannath Temple: state tourism account of the complex and living traditions
source_title: Shree Jagannath Temple
publisher: Department of Tourism, Government of Odisha
text: Odisha Tourism describes Shree Jagannath Temple as a 12th-century temple built by Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva in the Kalinga style. Its page identifies Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra as the wooden deities and connects periodic renewal of the images with Nabakalebara, describing the interval as 12–19 years. It names the principal architectural components as the Vimana or sanctum, Jagamohan or assembly hall, Natyamandira or dance hall, Bhoga Mandapa or offering hall, and Singhadwara, and gives the shikhara height as 65 metres. The page also describes daily Mahaprasad preparation in earthen pots. These are claims of the state tourism page and remain pending source review; the page does not establish temple-specific inscriptions or conservation history.

title: Puri Ratha Jatra: rituals and the 2026 Odisha Tourism calendar
source_title: Puri Ratha Jatra 2026 & Chariot Festival
publisher: Department of Tourism, Government of Odisha
text: Odisha Tourism's Ratha Jatra page describes the annual procession in which Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra leave the Shree Mandir and travel along Bada Danda toward Gundicha Temple. It names Pahandi, Chhera Pahanra, Gundicha Jatra, Bahuda Jatra, Suna Besha and Niladri Bije, and says the deities stay at Gundicha Temple for seven days before the return journey. The page presents the account of the deities' illness after Deba Snana Purnima and Gundicha as an aunt's home as religious tradition, not as historical evidence. Its calendar is specifically for 2026: it lists Ratha Jatra on 16 July, Bahuda on 24 July and Niladri Bije on 27 July. These dates are an archived 2026 schedule, not a future timetable. The page does not supply temple-specific epigraphic evidence.

title: Kashi Vishwanath Temple: official FAQ visitor timings and named observances
source_title: FAQ — Shri Kashi Vishwanath Temple
text: The temple administration FAQ PDF lists general temple opening hours as 03:00–23:00 and darshan windows as 04:00–11:00, 12:20–19:00 and 20:30–21:00. It lists Mangala Aarti at 03:00–04:00, Midday/Bhog Aarti at 11:15–12:20, Sapta-Rishi Aarti at 19:00–20:15 and Night/Shringar Aarti at 21:00–22:15. In its FAQ answer on functions and festivals, it names Rangbhari Ekadashi, Diwali, monthly Shivratri, Mahashivratri and the month of Kartik. The PDF also states that ordinary entry has no fee while special darshan has a charge; because these arrangements are time-sensitive, check the temple's current official portal before travel rather than relying on this document as a live notice. The PDF table of contents points to temple timing on page 4 and festivals on page 8. No publication date is stated in the inspected PDF text; accessed 2026-11-05.

title: Lepakshi Veerabhadra Temple: development, architecture, inscriptions and tentative heritage status
source_title: Sri Veerabhadra Temple and Monolithic Bull (Nandi), Lepakshi (The Vijayanagara Sculpture and Painting Art Tradition)
publisher: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Tentative List submission by India)
text: India's UNESCO Tentative List dossier describes the Lepakshi Veerabhadra temple complex as a multi-phase site. It proposes broad architectural phases from 1100–1350, 1350–1600 and 1600–1800 CE; the dossier associates the complex's mature Vijayanagara development with the period of Achyutaraya (1529–1542). It cautions that inscriptions do not establish the temple's early history. The dossier describes a three-shrine arrangement for Veerabhadra, Papanaseswara and Raghunatha, mandapas within successive enclosure walls, and fresco-secco paintings on plaster depicting epic and Puranic scenes. It reports about 20 inscriptions on enclosure walls, most associated with Achyutaraya's reign, and describes granite monolithic sculpture including the Nandi and Naga-sivalinga. Traditional narratives in the dossier, including the Jatayu account, are religious tradition rather than documentary history. Heritage status: this is a UNESCO Tentative List nomination submitted by India on 17 February 2022; it is not a World Heritage inscription. The dossier also records past damage to frescoes from long periods without maintenance, but it is not a current conservation-condition report. Sources: UNESCO Tentative List dossier, accessed 2026-11-05, historical narrative and component descriptions (web page; no PDF page numbers).

title: Chennakesavami Temple, Sompalle: ASI report on history, structure, worship and repairs
source_title: Archaeological Survey of India Annual Report 1902-03: Chennakesavami Temple at Sompalle
publisher: Archaeological Survey of India; digitized by IGNCA
text: The Archaeological Survey of India's 1902–03 annual report records the local Poligar-family account of Sompalle's development and temple building; the report presents this as local tradition, not independently established chronology. Its description identifies the main image as Chennakesavami and records daily puja at the time of the report, with copper processional images of the deity and Sri Devi and Bhudevi used on festival occasions. Architecturally, the report calls the building Vijayanagara style and describes a single enclosed court, east gateway with stone lower section and brick-and-plaster superstructure, mukha mandapa, maha mandapa, ardha mandapa, kalyana mandapa, ratha-like shrine and a tall monolithic flagstaff. It notes a Telugu inscription in the utsava-image mandapa naming a donor, Krishnama Nayudu, and a cyclic-year date but the digitized passage does not securely resolve the corresponding calendar year. The report describes earlier repairs to damaged brickwork, roof leakage and structural elements; these are historical conservation observations from the early twentieth century and do not establish present condition. Report reference: pages 85–89 (printed pagination), accessed 2026-11-05. The report's historical place names and descriptions are retained as period terminology, not asserted as current administrative data.

title: Golingeswara group at Biccavolu: Eastern Chalukya-era architecture and sculpture
source_title: Sri Golingeswara Swami Vari Temple, Biccavolu
publisher: East Godavari District Administration, Government of Andhra Pradesh
text: The East Godavari District Administration page describes Biccavolu as a group of Eastern Chalukya-period temples and dates the group broadly to the 9th–10th centuries; it uses the village's older form Birudankinavolu and associates the place with Gunaga Vijayaditya III. Its account of Golingeswara identifies a central Shiva shrine, a Sivalinga, and 33 inscriptional lines on the door jambs. It describes the mukhamandapa sculptures of Shiva with Parvati (Alingana Chandrasekhara) and Ganesha, and records named images and features in nearby Rajaraja and Chandrasekhara shrines. The page also discusses field temples and loose sculptures, but does not provide a decipherment or translation of the 33-line inscription, a festival calendar, or current visitor arrangements. The page is an official district account with no publication date shown; accessed 2026-11-05. Its broad dating and historical attribution are preserved as claims of that page and remain pending review.

title: Hemavati Group of Old Temples: conservation work items listed by the National Culture Fund
source_title: Amaravati Circle Joint Hand: Andhra Pradesh
publisher: National Culture Fund / Archaeological Survey of India project listing
text: The National Culture Fund's Amaravati Circle listing includes the Group of Old Temples at Hemavati, Sri Sathya Sai District, and describes work items for the site: stucco treatment to a brick minaret over the enclosure wall and a subsidiary-shrine vimana, pointing of masonry, underpinning of a brick wall, water-tightening of sub-shrines, illumination, and replacement of an old toilet block with a pilgrim toilet block. The page is a project/work listing; it does not state when each item was completed, so these are recorded as listed conservation works rather than confirmed completed repairs. It provides no historical chronology, deity identification, inscription reading, festival details or current visitor rules. Accessed 2026-11-05; no publication date displayed.

title: Gudimallam Parasuramesvara Temple: development-plan description and 2011 TTD proposal
source_title: Tirupati Urban Development Authority Master Plan and Zonal Development Plans 2040, Part A
text: The Tirupati Urban Development Authority's regional plan identifies the Sri Parsurameshwara Temple at Gudimallam as a religious site, lists ASI ownership with Endowments Department functioning, and describes a stone-and-lime structure with an off-axis entrance, semi-vaulted roof and walled mandapa. The same plan labels the period as the 2nd century and style as Early Chola, while a 2011 TTD board agenda describes worship of the linga as dating to the 2nd century BCE; these source statements are not identical in scope or precision and require specialist review rather than being collapsed into a single uncontested date. The TTD agenda says maintenance was then with the Archaeology Department and proposes that TTD take over; the document alone does not establish that the proposal was carried out. The TUDA plan also notes conservation status as “GOOD” in its own assessment, which is historical and not a current condition survey. TUDA PDF page 78; TTD agenda item 269, resolution dated 2011-01-20; both accessed 2026-11-05.

title: Lepakshi Veerabhadra Temple: ASI conservation work recorded in 1956-57
source_title: Indian Archaeology 1956-57: A Review
publisher: Department of Archaeology, Government of India / Archaeological Survey of India
text: The Archaeological Survey of India's 1956-57 review records conservation work at the Virabhadra Temple, Lepakshi: central floor slabs were reset and open joints filled. This is a dated report of work undertaken in that review year, not a present-condition assessment or a full conservation history. Report reference: printed page 51; accessed 2026-11-05.

title: Lepakshi Basavanna Temple: ASI platform work recorded in 1956-57
source_title: Indian Archaeology 1956-57: A Review
publisher: Department of Archaeology, Government of India / Archaeological Survey of India
text: The Archaeological Survey of India's 1956-57 review states that a cut-stone facing platform was constructed for the colossal bull at the Basavanna Temple, Lepakshi. This records one specific intervention in the review year; the source does not describe the temple's wider history, deity traditions, festivals, or current condition. Report reference: printed page 51; accessed 2026-11-05.

title: Madhavaraya Temple, Gorantla: ASI mandapa roof conservation in 1956-57
source_title: Indian Archaeology 1956-57: A Review
publisher: Department of Archaeology, Government of India / Archaeological Survey of India
text: The Archaeological Survey of India's 1956-57 review records that the terraces of the mandapas at Madhavaraya Temple, Gorantla, were made watertight. This is a historical conservation entry for 1956-57; it does not establish the present roof condition or the temple's full architectural chronology. Report reference: printed page 51; accessed 2026-11-05.

title: Madhavaraya Swamy Temple, Gorantla: ASI drainage and perimeter flooring works in 2012-13
source_title: Indian Archaeology 2012-13: A Review
publisher: Archaeological Survey of India, Government of India
text: The Archaeological Survey of India's 2012-13 review reports granite flooring laid around the temple over a lime-concrete bed, following exposed original flooring members. It also records slopes and channels intended to drain rainwater away from the monument. This is a report of work documented for 2012-13, not a current condition survey. Report reference: printed page 278; accessed 2026-11-05.

title: Mallikarjuna Temple, Kambaduru: ASI compound-wall conservation in 1956-57
source_title: Indian Archaeology 1956-57: A Review
publisher: Department of Archaeology, Government of India / Archaeological Survey of India
text: The Archaeological Survey of India's 1956-57 review records that broken portions of the compound wall at Mallikarjuna Temple, Kambaduru, were made watertight and stabilized; recessed pointing was applied as a repair treatment to the cut stonework. These works are historical observations for the review year and should not be read as the monument's current condition. Report reference: printed page 51; accessed 2026-11-05.

title: Venkateswara Vishnu Temple, Mangapuram: ASI repair entry from 2012-13
source_title: Indian Archaeology 2012-13: A Review
publisher: Archaeological Survey of India, Government of India
text: The Archaeological Survey of India's 2012-13 review includes Venkateshwara Vishnu Temple, Mangapuram, in its preservation section and records repair work to damaged flooring in the temple's cloister mandapa at the south-east and north-east corners. The source does not specify the present condition or visitor arrangements. Report reference: printed pages 278-279; accessed 2026-11-05.

title: Chenna Keshava Swamy Temple, Sompalem: ASI work recorded in 2012-13
source_title: Indian Archaeology 2012-13: A Review
publisher: Archaeological Survey of India, Government of India
text: The Archaeological Survey of India's 2012-13 review records environmental beautification work around the monument, including a lawn bed within the protected area, under the printed name 'Sri Chenna Keshava Swamy Temple, Sompalem, District Chittor.' This is a dated site-management entry; it does not provide a temple history, festival calendar, or current visitor information. The catalogue locality is Sompalle; the spelling difference requires review. Report reference: printed page 279; accessed 2026-11-05.

title: Hayagriva Madhava Temple at Hajo: state tourism account of history, cultural significance and festivals
source_title: Hayagriva Madhava Temple
text: Assam Tourism places the Hayagriva Madhava Temple on Monikut Hill, 28 kilometres west of Guwahati, and describes its architecture as combining Hindu and Buddhist styles. The tourism page attributes construction to King Raghu Deva Narayan in 1583. It describes the temple as a place associated with interreligious pilgrimage and says Doul Utsav is celebrated at the adjacent Doul Griha; it also names Bihu and Janmashtami as annual observances at the temple. The source does not give an inscriptional basis for its construction attribution, a detailed architectural inventory, current timings or fees. The date and festival claims are the state tourism page's account and remain pending review. Accessed 2026-11-05.

title: Hayagriva Madhava and shared Hindu-Buddhist reverence in Hajo
source_title: Assam Tourism Coffee Table Book
text: Assam Tourism's 2018 coffee-table book describes Hayagriva-Madhava as a Vishnu shrine on Manikut Hill in Hajo and records a Buddhist tradition that identifies the temple image with Gautama Buddha. The account says Buddhist visitors, particularly from Bhutan, visit the shrine. This is reported as a religious interpretation and pilgrimage tradition, not as a historical identification established by archaeological evidence. The book situates the temple within Hajo's wider multi-faith landscape; that regional context is not used here to infer temple-specific rituals beyond what the source states. Accessed 2026-11-05. PDF reference: printed page 72.

title: Negheriting Shiva Doul: state tourism history, reconstruction and surrounding shrines
source_title: Assam Tourism Coffee Table Book
text: The Assam Tourism 2018 coffee-table book identifies Negheriting Shiva-dol as a stone temple in the Dergaon area and dates it broadly to the 9th century. The passage situates it in the wider Golaghat/Kaziranga region. The inspected source does not establish its builder, exact construction chronology, surrounding subsidiary shrines, festivals, inscriptions, or current visitor arrangements. The broad date is the state tourism publication's statement and remains pending human review. Accessed 2026-11-05. PDF reference: printed page 72.

title: Siva Dole at Sibsagar: Assam Tourism account of its Ahom-period setting
source_title: Assam Tourism Coffee Table Book
text: Assam Tourism's 2018 coffee-table book places the Shiva-dol in Sivasagar's historic landscape of temples and large water tanks. It describes Sivasagar as the former Ahom capital, refers to the Shiva-dol and adjacent Sivasagar Tank, and mentions Joy-dol, Vishnu-dol and Devi-dol among the area's other temples. The inspected passages give district context only; they do not provide a shrine-specific chronology or design description, and do not establish claims about the separately catalogued Gaurisagar or Joysagar temples. Accessed 2026-11-05. PDF reference: printed pages 66 and 72.

temple_name: Shri Surya Pahar Ruins, Dasabhaja Devasthan
title: Suryapahar: Assam Tourism description of the multi-religious archaeological landscape
source_title: Assam Tourism Coffee Table Book
text: Assam Tourism's 2018 coffee-table book describes Suryapahar in Goalpara as a hillock archaeological site with Hindu, Buddhist and Jain remains. It reports numerous engraved Shiva lingas, Buddhist stupas and sculptures associated with Jain religious traditions, and interprets the material as evidence of a long-lived settlement. In a separate section it refers to granite Buddhist votive stupas and the coexistence of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain remains. The publication does not give a secure temple-by-temple chronology or identify the Dasabhaja Devasthan structure specifically in the inspected passage; those details remain research gaps. Accessed 2026-11-05. PDF reference: printed pages 66 and 72.

title: Ganesh Temple, Bharmour: Chaurasi complex and documented heritage context
source_title: Adopt a Heritage / Apni Dharohar Apni Pehchaan and Aaj Purani Rahon Se: Himachal Pradesh
publisher: Ministry of Tourism, Government of India; Himachal Pradesh project material
text: The inspected 2019 profile explicitly names the Ganesh Temple at Bharmour as one of the four Chaurasi shrines under ASI Shimla Circle jurisdiction. A 2019 Government of India tourism-project profile describes the Chaurasi temple complex at Bharmour as a group of 84 shrines and names this temple among four shrines under ASI Shimla Circle jurisdiction. The profile attributes patronage of the four named shrines to Meru Varmana, described there as an early Varman ruler of Bharmour (then called Bramhapur), and connects the shrines with the cultural history of Chamba and the Manimahesh pilgrimage. These are statements in the project profile. The brief account does not supply a separate, detailed description for each shrine. Accessed 2026-11-05. title: Harihareshvara Temple, Harihar: Hoysala-period history, inscriptions and architecture
source_title: World Heritage Site Nomination Dossier: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (Supplementary Information)
publisher: Government of India / Government of Karnataka, submitted to UNESCO World Heritage Centre
text: The supplementary inventory in the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas nomination dossier identifies the Harihareshvara Temple at Harihar, in the dossier's spelling Devanagere, as a living temple dedicated to Harihara, the combined form of Shiva and Vishnu. The dossier dates the building to 1224 CE and attributes its commissioning to Polalva, a general of Hoysala king Narasimha II. It reports that inscriptions record endowments by the Pandya rulers of Uchchangi and Vijayanagara rulers; it does not reproduce those inscriptions here. The building is described as chloritic-schist stone, granite and brick masonry, with an indented sanctum, antarala, navaranga and mahamandapa arranged east–west. The northern and southern entrances lead to porches; the north porch was extended and adapted as an antarala for a subsidiary shrine. The dossier describes a 1.21-metre Harihara image whose two halves carry Vishnu's chakra and conch and Shiva's trident and rosary. A Lakshmi shrine adjoins the main sanctum, and another Hariharesvara shrine is built into the west enclosure wall. It counts 56 circular lathe-turned pillars supporting an S-shaped eave and characterizes the plan as an ekakuta with a semi-stellate pattern. The dossier says the monument is protected and maintained by ASI and that worship/festivals are managed by Karnataka's MUZRAI department, but supplies no festival names or calendar. This temple appears in supplementary inventory material; that inclusion alone does not make it one of the three components inscribed as the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas. Source section inspected, printed pages 16–17 (PDF lines 3124–3168); accessed 5 November 2026.

title: Isvara Temple, Arsikere: Hoysala patronage, shrines and stellate design
source_title: World Heritage Site Nomination Dossier: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (Supplementary Information)
publisher: Government of India / Government of Karnataka, submitted to UNESCO World Heritage Centre
text: The Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas supplementary inventory describes Isvara Temple at Arsikere as a living Shiva temple built in chloritic schist and attributes it to Hoysala king Vira Ballala II, giving 1220 CE as its establishment date. Its account distinguishes an ekakuta shrine with an open mukha-mandapa from a dvikuta shrine with a shared pillared mandapa, all within a compound wall. It names the Shiva forms in the shrines as Chandramoulesvara, Veereshvara and Bakkeshvara. The main shrine sequence includes a porch, closed navaranga, open antarala and sanctum. The dossier emphasizes an unusual combination of stellate plans: a sixteen-pointed star plan in both sanctum and mukha-mandapa, with differing profiles, and a five-tier Vesara superstructure following the sanctum's plan. It also describes varied ceiling types and a highly ornamented six-tier domed ceiling in the mukha-mandapa, as well as sculpted exterior walls. These descriptions are the dossier authors' architectural interpretation and are not a separate UNESCO inscription or recognition of this individual temple. The inspected section supplies no festival calendar, current visitor timings, or entry information. Source section inspected, printed pages 18–20 (PDF lines 3171–3222); accessed 5 November 2026.

title: Lakshmidevi Temple, Doddagadavalli: foundation, four-spired plan and iconography
source_title: World Heritage Site Nomination Dossier: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (Supplementary Information)
publisher: Government of India / Government of Karnataka, submitted to UNESCO World Heritage Centre
text: The supplementary inventory for the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas identifies Lakshmidevi Temple at Doddagadavalli (the catalogue locality is spelled Doddgaddavalli) as a living temple made of chloritic schist. It says merchant Kullahana Rahuta and his wife Sajajadevi commissioned it in 1113 CE and calls it one of the oldest recognizably Hoysala temples. The dossier records historic names for the settlement—Gadduballi, Dakshina Kollapurava and Abhinava Kollapura—while its comparison with the Kolhapur Mahalakshmi site is contextual rather than proof of a direct institutional relationship. The compound is described as centered on a four-spired chatushkuta shrine aligned to cardinal directions, with four smaller corner shrines on the compound wall aligned to ordinal directions. The dossier also notes an eastern pillared entrance with dvarapalas and a western Bhairava shrine it considers a later addition. Two ceiling panels depict the ashtadikpalakas. The dossier distinguishes sculptural modes and discusses images including Mahalakshmi, Mahakali and a possibly identified Bhutanatha linga; it reports that only three of nine original cult images remain intact and says the Virabhadra now in the south-facing Vishnu shrine is a recent replacement, without dating that replacement. Its phrase “Kadamba Nagara” is presented as a label sometimes used, while the dossier discusses Early Chalukyan resonances and competing stylistic interpretations. The temple's appearance in a supplementary nomination inventory does not mean that this individual temple is itself a component of the property inscribed in 2023. The inspected section provides no current festival schedule, opening hours, or fees. Source section inspected, printed pages 33–35 (PDF lines 3519–3568); accessed 5 November 2026.

title: Viranarayana Temple, Belavadi: three-shrine Hoysala plan and sculptural program
source_title: World Heritage Site Nomination Dossier: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (Supplementary Information)
publisher: Government of India / Government of Karnataka, submitted to UNESCO World Heritage Centre
text: The supplementary inventory in the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas nomination dossier describes Viranarayana Temple at Belavadi as a living Vaishnava temple in chloritic schist. It gives 1206 CE and reports the attribution to Hoysala king Veera Ballala or Narasimha Ballala as coming from the head priest; this is retained as an attributed account rather than independent inscriptional proof. The dossier describes the present temple as a trikuta (three-celled) complex that developed from an earlier ekakuta plan. It identifies the western main shrine with Veera Narayana, the southern subsidiary shrine with Venu Gopala and the northern one with Yoga Narasimha. The dossier suggests, rather than proves, that the additions occurred in phases, and says the side-shrine arrangement may reflect the popularity of Venu Gopala and Narasimha forms. The shrine complex has an eastern main entrance, an antarala, a closed navaranga and a semi-open mandapa. The Yoga Narasimha shrine has a semi-stellate plan, while the two other shrine plans are linear; the three Vesara superstructures follow those distinct profiles. The inventory contrasts the plain exterior of the central western shrine with figure sculpture on the side shrines, and notes varied pillar forms, polished lathe-turned pillars and elephant figures supporting the kakshasana seats. It also mentions serial Bhagavata scenes among dancers and musicians on the exterior seating backrest. The report calls the site ASI centrally protected and states that from 1760 the temple was under Sringeri Matha, which paid daily worship expenses; these are reported in the dossier and are not current administrative details. The dossier's appearance as supplementary inventory should not be confused with individual inscription on the World Heritage List: the inscribed serial property's components are three other named temples. Source section inspected, printed pages 29–32 (PDF lines 3446–3493); accessed 5 November 2026.

text: The Assam Directorate of Tourism describes the surviving feature at Da-Parbatia near Tezpur as the ruins of a temple doorway. The door jambs are described as bearing figures of the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna, each holding a garland, among decorative foliage. title: Sivadol, Gaurisagar: Ahom patronage and temple architecture
source_title: 31. Sivadol, Gaurisagar
publisher: Archaeological Survey of India, Guwahati Circle
text: The Archaeological Survey of India's Guwahati Circle profile says Sivadol at Gaurisagar was constructed by Phuleswari Devi, queen of Ahom king Siba Singha (CE 1714–1744), and dedicated to Shiva. It describes brick masonry, a garbhagriha and mukhamandapa, with the sanctum floor lower than the mandapa floor. The domical sikhara has vertical ridges and subsidiary angasikharas. ASI places the temple in the middle of a group of three temples on the northern bank of the Gaurisagar tank and notes an enclosing wall. The profile gives locality and approach information, but does not name festivals, provide visitor hours or establish a current visitor policy. Accessed 5 November 2026.

title: Sivadol, Gaurisagar: conservation work reported for 2000–01
source_title: Indian Archaeology 2000–01: A Review
publisher: Archaeological Survey of India / National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities
text: The Archaeological Survey of India's 2000–01 annual review reports that decayed lime-concrete plaster on Sivadol's mandapa roof was replaced with matching plaster. It also records construction of a two-metre-wide brick-paved visitor path and restoration of the ancient compound walls on two sides using combination mortar. These are works reported for that specific reporting period; the report does not establish the temple's present condition or current visitor arrangements. Accessed 5 November 2026.

title: Vishnudol, Gaurisagar: Ahom-period patronage and temple plan
source_title: 30. Vishnudol, Gaurisagar
publisher: Archaeological Survey of India, Guwahati Circle
text: The Archaeological Survey of India's Guwahati Circle identifies this monument as Vishnudol at Gaurisagar and says it was built by Siba Singha (CE 1714–1744) and dedicated to Vishnu. The catalogue record uses the names Bisdol (Bishnudol) (Gaurisagar); the ASI profile's Vishnudol spelling and Gaurisagar location are the basis for associating this evidence with that existing record. ASI describes brick masonry and a nilachala type domical sikhara with a honeycomb design. The plan comprises an octagonal garbhagriha, square mandapa and intervening antarala; the outer walls carry figures of divinities and the temple stands within an enclosure wall. The profile does not provide a festival calendar or current visitor details. Accessed 5 November 2026.

It attributes the temple's construction to Raja Sahil Varman and says it was built in memory of his daughter Champavati. The passage provides no architectural description, deity identification, festival calendar, inscriptions, conservation account or current visitor timings. title: Panchvaktra Temple, Mandi: ASI inventory account of history and architecture
source_title: Panchvaktra Temple (Mandi), monument inventory entry 118
publisher: Archaeological Survey of India record hosted by Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts
source_page_reference: PDF entry 118; notification reference F-4-1/52-A2 dated 28 July 1952; PDF text lines 2725–2735
text: The ASI monument-inventory entry identifies Panchvaktra as a Shiva temple in Mandi and describes it as a stone temple in the northern shikhara style. It notes a mandapa supported on four heavy pillars with pot-and-foliage ornament. The entry says an earlier temple at the site was destroyed by floods in the early eighteenth century and that Raja Sidhanath built the present temple at the same spot; it also assigns the temple to the fifteenth century. The source does not explain the chronology between these statements, so this profile preserves the source's ambiguity rather than reconciling it. It describes a subsidiary temple to the west as having the same design and date. The inventory lists government ownership, continuing religious use, ASI Chandigarh Circle administrative control and notification reference F-4-1/52-A2 dated 28 July 1952. Its approach fields name Shimla airport, Jogindernagar railway station and Mandi bus station, but these are inventory directions rather than a current transport advisory. Accessed 5 November 2026.

title: Panchvaktra Temple: flood-protection work reported in 2012–13
source_title: Indian Archaeology 2012–13: A Review
publisher: Archaeological Survey of India / National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities
source_page_reference: Printed page 317; section 330; PDF text lines 9022–9023
text: The Archaeological Survey of India's 2012–13 review says work was in progress to reduce the risk of Beas River floodwaters entering Panchvaktra Temple. It reports that a retaining wall was provided on the river side and strengthened with concealed reinforced-concrete columns and tie-beams, with granular filling behind the wall toward the temple. This is a dated account of work in progress, not evidence that the work was completed or that it describes the present condition of the temple. Accessed 5 November 2026.
